q: What serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level defines vitamin D sufficiency per the American Geriatrics Society (used for fall/fracture prevention in frail older adults)?
explanation:
The AGS definition used for fall and fracture prevention in frail high-risk older adults is serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D greater than 30 ng/mL (p1539).

B. Greater than 20 ng/mL: This is the Institute of Medicine sufficiency definition for general-population bone health (p1539).
C. 12 to 20 ng/mL: The Institute of Medicine defines this as insufficiency (p1539).
A. Less than 12 ng/mL: The Institute of Medicine defines this as deficiency (p1539).

q: Does TSH rising with normal aging indicate occult thyroid failure?
o: Yes - normal aging generally lowers free T4 as TSH rises
Yes - rising TSH with stable free T4 proves occult failure
No - TSH generally decreases in euthyroid aging without underlying thyroid disease
No - free T4 remains unchanged in euthyroid aging
explanation: TSH gradually rises with age while free T4 remains unchanged in euthyroid people without thyroid disease (p1546). Declining free T4, occult failure despite stable free T4, and declining TSH each contradict this pattern.

q: A patient on 112 μg levothyroxine daily has a rising TSH. Before assuming disease progression, what simple explanation should be checked?
o: An unchanged average dose despite missing a weekly tablet
Absence of a TSH response to missed replacement doses
Missed doses and difficulty with adherence
Increased exposure from missing a weekly tablet
explanation:
Adherence should be considered first when TSH varies; missing one weekly dose of 112 micrograms reduces the daily average to 96 micrograms (p1552).

A. An unchanged average dose despite missing a weekly tablet: The prescribed 112-microgram dose does not ensure the delivered average if doses are missed (p1552).
D. Increased exposure from missing a weekly tablet: The example lowers the average from 112 to 96 micrograms (p1552).
B. Absence of a TSH response to missed replacement doses: The text discusses TSH elevation after stabilization and checking adherence and interacting conditions (p1552).

q: In managing myxedema coma, what is the critical sequencing error to avoid regarding hydrocortisone and thyroid hormone?
o: Initiating hydrocortisone to cover potentially impaired adrenal reserve
Giving thyroid hormone without hydrocortisone when adrenal reserve is impaired
Obtaining serum for cortisol measurement before starting hydrocortisone
Stopping hydrocortisone after the cortisol level is found adequate
explanation:
Thyroid hormone without hydrocortisone can precipitate adrenal crisis when adrenal reserve is impaired in myxedema coma (p1553).

C. Obtaining serum for cortisol measurement before starting hydrocortisone: The book recommends obtaining serum and then initiating IV hydrocortisone (p1553).
A. Initiating hydrocortisone to cover potentially impaired adrenal reserve: This is the recommended protection against adrenal crisis (p1553).
D. Stopping hydrocortisone after the cortisol level is found adequate: The book permits stopping it once cortisol is found adequate (p1553).

q: What total score on the 2010 ACR/EULAR RA classification criteria defines "definite RA"?
explanation:
As printed in Table 101-1, a score greater than 6 classifies definite rheumatoid arthritis (p1608).

A. Exactly 5 total points: Five is the table score for more than 10 involved joints including a small joint, not its printed definite-disease threshold (p1608).
B. Exactly 3 total points: Three is a component score, not the printed total-score threshold for definite disease (p1608).
C. Exactly 2 total points: Two is a component score for 1-3 small joints, not the printed definite-disease threshold (p1608).

q: How useful is anti-CCP antibody testing for distinguishing LORA from polymyalgia rheumatica?
o: One small study found the same positivity in LORA, PMR and healthy older controls
One small study found positivity in 65% of PMR but none of LORA or healthy controls
One small study found positivity in every LORA patient and none of the PMR patients
One small study found positivity in 65% of LORA but none of PMR or healthy controls
explanation:
In one small study, anti-CCP was positive in 65% of LORA patients but none of the PMR patients or healthy older controls, suggesting usefulness as a discriminator (p1611).

B. One small study found positivity in 65% of PMR but none of LORA or healthy controls: The 65% result belongs to LORA, not PMR (p1611).
C. One small study found positivity in every LORA patient and none of the PMR patients: The LORA result was 65%, not universal positivity (p1611).
A. One small study found the same positivity in LORA, PMR and healthy older controls: The groups differed: 65% in LORA and none in the other two groups (p1611).

q: What RA-specific risk requires evaluation before intubating a patient with long-standing disease?
o: Protection of the cervical spine by long-standing RA
Overextension as a means to prevent spinal-cord compromise
Absence of cervical risk after more than 10 years of RA
Cervical spine disease and atlantoaxial joint instability
explanation:
Long-standing RA can cause cervical spine disease and atlantoaxial instability, making overextension during intubation hazardous (p1612).

A. Protection of the cervical spine by long-standing RA: The book describes increased risk of cervical disease and instability (p1612).
C. Absence of cervical risk after more than 10 years of RA: More than 10 years of RA is identified as a particular risk setting (p1612).
B. Overextension as a means to prevent spinal-cord compromise: Overextension can compromise the brainstem or spinal cord (p1612).

q: How much more likely are Sjögren syndrome patients to develop lymphoma compared to matched controls?
o: Two to five times more likely
explanation:
Patients with Sjogren syndrome are 44 times more likely to develop lymphoma than matched normal subjects (p1626).

A. Two to five times more likely: This is the hematologic-malignancy risk in RA (p1626).
C. Two times more likely: This is the lymphoma risk with azathioprine or cyclosporin in RA relative to RA controls (p1626).
B. 50 times more likely: This is the non-Hodgkin lymphoma incidence in renal-transplant patients (p1626).
chapterTitle: Rheumatoid Arthritis and Other Autoimmune Diseases

q: What percentage of vertebral compression fractures are actually symptomatic?
explanation:
Only approximately 30% to 40% of vertebral compression fractures are symptomatic (p1631).

A. Approximately 93%: 93% is degenerative disc disease in one asymptomatic over-60 imaging sample, not symptomatic compression fractures (p1636).
C. Approximately 52%: 52% is disc bulge in one asymptomatic MRI study, not symptomatic compression fractures (p1636).
D. Approximately 21%: 21% is spinal stenosis in an asymptomatic over-60 sample, not symptomatic compression fractures (p1636).

q: Roughly what proportion of patients who sustain one vertebral fracture will have another within 5 years?
explanation:
Studies suggest over 20% of patients sustaining a fracture have another fracture within five years (p1631).

D. Approximately 30% to 40%: This is the approximate fraction of vertebral compression fractures that are symptomatic (p1631).
B. Approximately 93%: This is degenerative disc disease prevalence in an asymptomatic over-60 imaging sample (p1636).
C. Approximately 52%: This is the SPORT nonoperative-to-surgery crossover fraction at eight years (p1639).

q: In older adults, what is a key pitfall in recognizing infectious back pain (eg, discitis/osteomyelitis)?
o: Endovascular infection risk makes a mechanical cause more likely than spinal infection
Disc infection usually presents differently enough from mechanical disease to be recognized clinically
Fever can be absent despite spinal infection
Fever is generally required before spinal infection should enter the differential
explanation: Spinal infection can mimic mechanical disc disease and fever can be absent. High endovascular-infection risk should increase suspicion of a spinal infectious cause (p1631). Mechanical attribution from that risk, reliable clinical separation, and requiring fever are wrong.

q: How do you distinguish neurogenic claudication from vascular claudication on exercise testing?
o: Both conditions resolve on the treadmill because spinal extension increases canal diameter
Both conditions improve on the bicycle because spinal flexion reduces vascular symptoms
Neurogenic symptoms improve on the bicycle; vascular symptoms persist on both tests
Neurogenic symptoms persist on both tests; vascular symptoms improve on the bicycle
explanation:
Neurogenic claudication worsens on the treadmill and improves on a bicycle; vascular claudication persists with both tests (p1636).

D. Neurogenic symptoms persist on both tests; vascular symptoms improve on the bicycle: This reverses the stated distinction (p1636).
B. Both conditions improve on the bicycle because spinal flexion reduces vascular symptoms: Vascular claudication causes persistent difficulty on both tests (p1636).
A. Both conditions resolve on the treadmill because spinal extension increases canal diameter: Spinal flexion during cycling increases canal diameter; neurogenic symptoms worsen on the treadmill (p1636).

q: Why is lumbar spine imaging a poor stand-alone diagnostic tool in older adults?
o: A herniated nucleus pulposus generally establishes the cause of the presenting symptoms
Lumbar imaging abnormalities are common in asymptomatic older adults
A disc bulge on MRI is usually sufficient to attribute the clinical pain to that level
Disc degeneration is uncommon among asymptomatic people older than 60
explanation: Lumbar MRI often shows abnormalities in asymptomatic older adults, including disc bulges, protrusions and degeneration (p1636). Thus a herniation or bulge does not establish symptom causation, and degeneration is not uncommon in asymptomatic older people. The unchanged key states this diagnostic limitation.

q: In the epidural steroid injection RCT of 400 older adults with lumbar spinal stenosis, what did adding glucocorticoid to lidocaine achieve?
o: Proof that lidocaine alone has no effect compared with placebo
Minimal or no additional short-term disability or leg-pain benefit
Proof that steroid injections outperform a placebo injection
A clear additional short-term disability and leg-pain benefit
explanation:
The 400-patient trial found minimal or no additional short-term disability or leg-pain benefit from adding glucocorticoid to lidocaine; it had no placebo arm (p1639).

D. A clear additional short-term disability and leg-pain benefit: The reported comparison showed minimal or no short-term benefit (p1639).
C. Proof that steroid injections outperform a placebo injection: The trial included no placebo group (p1639).
A. Proof that lidocaine alone has no effect compared with placebo: Without a placebo arm, that comparison was not made (p1639).

q: In the SPORT trial, what fraction of the nonoperative arm had crossed over to surgery by 8 years?
explanation:
At eight-year SPORT follow-up, 52% of those randomized to nonoperative treatment had undergone surgery (p1639).

A. 36%: This is herniated nucleus pulposus prevalence in an asymptomatic over-60 MRI sample (p1636).
C. 21%: This is spinal stenosis prevalence in that asymptomatic sample (p1636).
D. 93%: This is degenerative disc disease prevalence in that sample (p1636).
retiredReason: Number recall from one passage; not exam-style.

q: Why doesn't "start low, go slow" apply to antibiotic dosing in older adults?
o: Older adults generally need a reduced initial dose because faster antibiotic absorption raises blood levels
Serious-infection outcomes depend on quickly reaching therapeutic antibiotic levels
Renal and hepatic function generally have little relevance when adjusting later antibiotic doses
Serious-infection outcomes improve when therapeutic levels are deliberately delayed
explanation: For serious infections, prompt therapeutic antibiotic levels determine outcome: use a full initial dose and adjust subsequent doses for renal/hepatic function and interactions (p1667). Reducing the initial dose because of faster absorption, disregarding later organ-function adjustment, and deliberately delaying therapeutic levels are wrong.

q: What dosing frequency threshold is associated with reduced antibiotic adherence?
explanation:
Antibiotic regimens requiring more than twice-daily dosing are associated with reduced adherence rates (p1670).

A. Twice-daily or less frequent dosing: The reported association is with greater than twice-daily dosing (p1670).
B. No dosing-frequency threshold: The book explicitly identifies greater than twice-daily dosing (p1670).
D. Increasing frequency always improves adherence: The reported association goes in the opposite direction above twice daily (p1670).

q: How much higher is early (30-day) sepsis mortality in adults over 65 compared with younger adults?
explanation:
Early sepsis mortality within 30 days is 50% higher in adults older than 65 than in younger adults (p1671).

A. 45% higher: 45% is the increase in endocarditis diagnostic yield with TEE over TTE in seniors (p1671).
D. 55% higher: 55% is fever prevalence in older adults with endocarditis, not the sepsis mortality increase (p1671).
C. 25% higher: 25% is leukocytosis prevalence in older adults with endocarditis, not the sepsis mortality increase (p1671).

q: Roughly what proportion of pneumonia in older adults is caused by *S pneumoniae*?
explanation:
Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common pneumonia agent in older adults, accounting for 20% to 65% of cases (p1681).

A. 12% to 18%: This is the smaller proportion involving viruses (p1681).
B. 5% to 10%: This is the lifetime risk of active TB in healthy people infected with TB, not pneumococcal pneumonia frequency (p1692).
D. Over 90%: This is pneumococcal urinary-antigen specificity, not etiologic frequency (p1685).

q: What serum lactate cutoff predicts 30-day mortality in older adults with pneumonia?
o: No serum lactate cutoff is described
Any lactate value, without a threshold
explanation:
Serum lactate of at least 2 mmol/L predicts 30-day mortality in older adults with pneumonia (p1685).

C. Below 2 mmol/L: This reverses the reported threshold direction (p1685).
A. No serum lactate cutoff is described: The book specifies greater than or equal to 2 mmol/L (p1685).
B. Any lactate value, without a threshold: The predictor is stated with a threshold of at least 2 mmol/L (p1685).

q: Why should quinolones be avoided when active pulmonary tuberculosis is suspected but not yet confirmed?
o: Their early use generally establishes tuberculosis as the diagnosis before testing is completed
Their activity generally leaves the timing of pulmonary tuberculosis diagnosis unchanged
Their tuberculostatic activity can delay tuberculosis diagnosis
Their use for suspected Legionella is generally discouraged in the pneumonia regimen described
explanation: Quinolones have tuberculostatic activity that may delay pulmonary-TB diagnosis. If Legionella cannot be ruled out, the chapter includes a respiratory quinolone or macrolide with a beta-lactam (p1689). Establishing TB early, leaving diagnosis timing unchanged, and discouraging the described Legionella use are wrong.

q: Does pyuria convert asymptomatic bacteriuria into symptomatic UTI?
o: No - pyuria generally indicates that the urine is free of bacteria
No - asymptomatic bacteriuria can occur with or without pyuria
Yes - pyuria is generally sufficient to classify bacteriuria as symptomatic infection
Yes - bacteria detected in urine are generally classified as symptomatic infection
explanation: ASB is bacteriuria with or without pyuria in the absence of localizing signs or symptoms (p1699). Pyuria does not imply bacteria are absent; neither pyuria nor bacteriuria alone establishes symptomatic infection. Only the unchanged key retains the symptom distinction.

q: What distinguishes simple cystitis from complicated UTI in this chapter?
o: Simple cystitis is bladder-confined; complicated UTI extends beyond the bladder
Complicated UTI is defined by symptoms confined to the bladder
Pyuria generally establishes complicated UTI without determining the infection location
Simple cystitis involves renal parenchyma; complicated UTI is bladder-confined
explanation: Simple cystitis has symptoms confined to the bladder; complicated UTI extends beyond it (p1700). Bladder-confined symptoms do not define complicated UTI, pyuria does not determine location, and the reversed bladder/renal-parenchymal classification is wrong.

q: Does a high postvoid residual consistently predict symptomatic UTI?
o: Yes - prospective studies generally confirmed increased symptomatic UTI with high residuals
Yes - a high residual is generally sufficient evidence of symptomatic urinary infection
No - the cited case-control study found a lower frequency of high residuals in recurrent UTI
No - prospective studies did not consistently find an association
explanation: High residuals have not consistently predicted symptomatic UTI. The cited case-control study found more high residuals with recurrent UTI, but prospective ambulatory and PALTC studies did not consistently confirm the association (p1702). Consistent prospective confirmation, residual alone diagnosing infection, and the reversed case-control result are wrong.

q: What ASB-treatment exception is specified for older adults?
o: For every asymptomatic older resident of a long-term-care facility
Before endoscopic urologic procedures associated with mucosal trauma
For a change in urine odor alone without localizing symptoms
explanation:
Screening for and treating ASB is recommended before endoscopic urologic procedures associated with mucosal trauma (p1703).

A. Whenever pyuria accompanies asymptomatic bacteriuria: ASB can include pyuria, and treatment is not recommended merely for bacteriuria in asymptomatic older adults (p1699, p1703).
B. For every asymptomatic older resident of a long-term-care facility: The guidance recommends against this except for specified urologic procedures (p1703).
D. For a change in urine odor alone without localizing symptoms: Urine-character change is insufficient to indicate UTI (p1705).

q: Should a urine color or odor change alone establish UTI?
o: Yes - diet and medication changes generally leave urine character unchanged
No - urine-character change alone is insufficient to indicate UTI
Yes - urine odor change is generally sufficient evidence of infection without urinary symptoms
No - mild dehydration generally leaves urine character unchanged
explanation: Urine-character change alone is insufficient for UTI and may reflect mild dehydration or diet/medication changes (p1705). The two claims that those alternatives leave urine unchanged and the claim that odor alone is sufficient are wrong.

q: Can an older man have simple cystitis?
o: Yes - men can have bladder-confined acute simple cystitis
No - first-line agents for male cystitis generally belong to different drug groups than those for women
No - male sex generally defines infection as extending beyond the bladder
Yes - infection extending beyond the bladder remains simple cystitis
explanation: The chapter treats acute simple cystitis in men and women; simple cystitis is bladder-confined and extension beyond it defines complicated UTI (pp1700,1710). Male sex does not establish extension, the first-line agents are similar, and an infection extending beyond the bladder is not simple cystitis.

q: When may a week of antibiotics suffice for an older man with simple cystitis?
o: When the response is delayed beyond the prompt-response interval
Whenever infection extends beyond the bladder, regardless of severity
Whenever fever persists, regardless of response to antibiotics
When the response is prompt, within 72 hours
explanation:
For most older men with acute simple cystitis, seven days is adequate if response is prompt, within 72 hours (p1711).

A. When the response is delayed beyond the prompt-response interval: The seven-day recommendation is conditional on prompt response; delayed response can justify longer treatment (p1710-1711).
C. Whenever fever persists, regardless of response to antibiotics: The text conditions the simple-cystitis recommendation on prompt response, and febrile UTI had different short-term outcomes (p1711).
B. Whenever infection extends beyond the bladder, regardless of severity: Complicated UTI requires management according to severity and is outside this simple-cystitis recommendation (p1711).

q: In the Tecumseh, Michigan, community study, what effect did immunizing 86% of children have on adult influenza rates?
o: Reduced adult influenza by a third
explanation:
In Tecumseh, immunizing 86% of children reduced adult influenza by a third compared with an adjacent community where children were not immunized (p1736).

D. Reduced adult influenza by 70% to 90%: 70%-90% is the prophylactic effectiveness of neuraminidase inhibitors, not the Tecumseh vaccination result (p1736).
A. Reduced adult influenza by 86%: 86% is the proportion of children immunized, not the adult reduction (p1736).
B. Reduced adult influenza by 54%: 54% is a reported epidemic influenza rate in schoolchildren, not the adult reduction in Tecumseh (p1736).
